--- title: "Cross-validation" description: "Why a single train/test split is too noisy to trust, how many folds to use, and why you may not quote the winning score from a search." order: 1 categories: [validation] --- ## Why this matters [Section 5](../05-generalisation/index.qmd) established that training error is not performance, and that you must measure on data the model has not seen. It then cheerfully broke its own rule on every page, choosing complexity by looking at the test set and saying so each time. This page fixes that. The problem with holding out a test set and looking at it is not philosophical fussiness — it is that a single held-out set is a *noisy* measurement, and looking at it repeatedly converts that noise into a systematically flattering answer. Cross-validation reduces the noise. Nesting the cross-validation removes the flattery. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## The idea A *fold* is a slice of the data. **k-fold cross-validation** cuts the data into $k$ equal slices, then fits the model $k$ times: each time, one slice is held out for scoring and the other $k - 1$ are used for fitting. Every observation is scored exactly once, by a model that never saw it. The $k$ scores are then combined into one number. You get two things a single split cannot give. The estimate uses *all* the data for scoring rather than a quarter of it, so it is far less noisy. And the spread of the $k$ fold-scores tells you how uncertain that estimate is — a standard error for your performance number, which a single split simply does not have. ## Worked example ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() rec <- recipe(abundance ~ ., data = d) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) spec <- rand_forest(trees = 300) |> set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |> set_mode("regression") wf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(spec) nrow(d) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 720 ``` ::: ::: ### How much does a single split actually tell you? The honest way to ask is to do it many times. We take forty different 75/25 splits of the same 720 stations, fit the same random forest to each, and look at the spread of the answers. Then we do the same for forty different ten-fold cross-validations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(7) single <- map_dfr(1:40, \(i) { sp <- initial_split(d, prop = 0.75) p <- augment(fit(wf, training(sp)), testing(sp)) tibble(scheme = "single 75/25 split", rep = i, rmse = rmse_vec(p$abundance, p$.pred), rsq = rsq_vec(p$abundance, p$.pred)) }) set.seed(8) crossval <- map_dfr(1:40, \(i) { m <- collect_metrics(fit_resamples(wf, vfold_cv(d, v = 10), metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq))) tibble(scheme = "10-fold cross-validation", rep = i, rmse = m$mean[m$.metric == "rmse"], rsq = m$mean[m$.metric == "rsq"]) }) estimates <- bind_rows(single, crossval) estimates |> summarise(across(c(rmse, rsq), list(mean = mean, sd = sd, lowest = min, highest = max)), .by = scheme) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|scheme | rmse_mean| rmse_sd| rmse_lowest| rmse_highest| rsq_mean| rsq_sd| rsq_lowest| rsq_highest| |:------------------------|---------:|-------:|-----------:|------------:|--------:|------:|----------:|-----------:| |single 75/25 split | 4.336| 0.418| 3.452| 5.453| 0.196| 0.057| 0.079| 0.346| |10-fold cross-validation | 4.277| 0.035| 4.200| 4.354| 0.216| 0.012| 0.195| 0.239|
::: ::: Nothing about the model changed between those eighty fits. The data did not change. Only the line drawn through it changed — and the answer moved by a factor of four. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimates |> mutate(scheme = factor(scheme, c("single 75/25 split", "10-fold cross-validation"))) |> ggplot(aes(rsq, y = 0, colour = scheme)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.3, alpha = 0.75, size = 2.4) + facet_wrap(~scheme, ncol = 1) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL, limits = c(-0.8, 0.8)) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("orange", "blue")])) + labs(x = expression(R^2~"on held-out stations"), y = NULL, title = "The same model, measured forty times each way") + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Forty estimates of the same model's R² from a single 75/25 split (top) and forty estimates from ten-fold cross-validation (bottom). Every point is the same random forest on the same 720 stations; the only difference is how the data were divided. The single-split estimates run from 0.079 to 0.346. The cross-validated estimates run from 0.195 to 0.239.](cross-validation_files/figure-html/fig-stability-1.png){#fig-stability fig-alt='Two horizontal strip plots sharing an x-axis labelled R-squared running from below 0.10 to 0.35. The upper strip, labelled single 75/25 split, shows forty orange points: most sit in a loose band between 0.14 and 0.24, with three stragglers down at 0.08 to 0.10 and four more out at 0.26, 0.28, 0.31 and 0.35. The lower strip, labelled ten-fold cross-validation, shows forty blue points packed into a single tight clump between 0.195 and 0.24, about a sixth of the width the orange points occupy, with no stragglers at all.' width=1400} ::: ::: A single split is not wrong. It is just imprecise, and the imprecision is large enough to reverse a comparison between two decent models. If you report R² = 0.34 from one lucky split and someone else reports 0.08 from one unlucky split, you have not disagreed about the ocean. ### How many folds? More folds means each model trains on more of the data, so the estimate is less pessimistic; it also means more fits. The extreme is **leave-one-out** cross-validation, where $k = n$ and each model is trained on all but a single station. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} formula_glm <- abundance ~ poly(depth_m, 2) + poly(temperature_c, 2) + log1p(chlorophyll_mg_m3) + salinity_psu + substrate + season fold_scores <- function(v) { parts <- map(vfold_cv(d, v = v)$splits, \(s) { m <- glm(formula_glm, data = analysis(s), family = poisson) tibble(obs = assessment(s)$abundance, pred = predict(m, assessment(s), type = "response")) }) all_at_once <- bind_rows(parts) c(pooled = rmse_vec(all_at_once$obs, all_at_once$pred), per_fold = mean(map_dbl(parts, \(p) rmse_vec(p$obs, p$pred)))) } fold_sweep <- map_dfr(c(2, 5, 10, 20), \(v) { set.seed(300 + v) map_dfr(1:25, \(i) as_tibble_row(fold_scores(v))) |> mutate(folds = v) }) fold_sweep |> summarise(`RMSE, pooled` = mean(pooled), `sd across repeats` = sd(pooled), `RMSE, averaged per fold` = mean(per_fold), .by = folds) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| folds| RMSE, pooled| sd across repeats| RMSE, averaged per fold| |-----:|------------:|-----------------:|-----------------------:| | 2| 4.307| 0.100| 4.302| | 5| 4.284| 0.044| 4.257| | 10| 4.278| 0.023| 4.223| | 20| 4.269| 0.017| 4.150|
::: ::: Read the first two numeric columns. Two folds is pessimistic — each model trains on only half the stations, and a Poisson model of counts genuinely does worse with 360 stations than with 648. By ten folds the bias has gone and the estimate has also become four times more stable across repeats. Going to twenty folds buys almost nothing for twice the work — and leave-one-out, at 720 fits, lands where five- and ten-fold already were: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} squared_errors <- map_dbl(seq_len(nrow(d)), \(i) { m <- glm(formula_glm, data = d[-i, ], family = poisson) (d$abundance[i] - predict(m, d[i, ], type = "response"))^2 }) c(`leave-one-out RMSE` = sqrt(mean(squared_errors))) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> leave-one-out RMSE #> 4.27 ``` ::: ::: That is the practical answer: **five or ten folds**, and ten is the usual default because the extra stability is cheap at this size. It is a convention, not a theorem, but on this dataset you can see why it became one. ::: {.callout-warning} ## The third column is not a different model `collect_metrics()` averages the RMSE of each fold. That is not the same as the RMSE of all the out-of-fold predictions pooled together, because the square root is taken before averaging instead of after. The gap grows with the number of folds — 0.005 at two folds, **0.119 at twenty** — for no reason connected to the model at all. So an RMSE reported from twenty-fold cross-validation is not comparable with one from five-fold, even for the same model on the same data. This is the same trap [section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) hit three times from a different direction, and the [regression measures page](regression-metrics.qmd) takes it apart properly. ::: ### May I quote the winning score? No, and this is the part that most often goes wrong in practice. Suppose we search for a good set of predictors. We add twenty columns of pure random noise to the data, draw 100 candidate models that each use five of the twenty-eight available columns, and score every one by ten-fold cross-validation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(21) noisy <- bind_cols(d, as_tibble(matrix(rnorm(nrow(d) * 20), nrow(d)), .name_repair = \(x) paste0("noise_", seq_along(x)))) predictors <- setdiff(names(noisy), "abundance") set.seed(23) candidates <- map(1:100, \(i) sample(predictors, 5)) cv_rmse <- function(data, vars, v, seed) { set.seed(seed) mean(map_dbl(vfold_cv(data, v = v)$splits, \(s) { m <- glm(reformulate(vars, "abundance"), data = analysis(s), family = poisson) rmse_vec(assessment(s)$abundance, predict(m, assessment(s), type = "response")) })) } searched <- map_dbl(candidates, \(v) cv_rmse(noisy, v, 10, 31)) winner <- candidates[[which.min(searched)]] c(best = min(searched), median = median(searched), worst = max(searched)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> best median worst #> 4.485 4.685 4.798 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} winner ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "longitude" "noise_20" "noise_18" "season" "noise_11" ``` ::: ::: The winning model uses three columns of pure noise out of five. Its cross-validated RMSE of 4.485 is the best of the hundred, and it is exactly the number that would appear in a paper. **Nested cross-validation** measures what that search is really worth. An outer set of folds is held back; inside each outer training set, the whole 100-candidate search is repeated from scratch on inner folds; the model that search picks is then scored on the outer fold, which the search never touched. To have something to compare against, we also score a fixed model — all eight real predictors, no search at all — on those same outer folds. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(32) outer_folds <- vfold_cv(noisy, v = 5) nested <- map_dfr(1:5, \(i) { train <- analysis(outer_folds$splits[[i]]) held <- assessment(outer_folds$splits[[i]]) inner <- map_dbl(candidates, \(v) cv_rmse(train, v, 5, 40 + i)) chosen <- candidates[[which.min(inner)]] on_held <- function(vars) { m <- glm(reformulate(vars, "abundance"), data = train, family = poisson) rmse_vec(held$abundance, predict(m, held, type = "response")) } tibble(fold = i, `search reported` = min(inner), `search's model, honestly` = on_held(chosen), `no search at all` = on_held(predictors[1:8]), `noise columns chosen` = sum(grepl("noise", chosen))) }) nested |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| fold| search reported| search's model, honestly| no search at all| noise columns chosen| |----:|---------------:|------------------------:|----------------:|--------------------:| | 1| 4.576| 4.001| 3.710| 3| | 2| 4.415| 5.358| 4.579| 2| | 3| 4.651| 4.663| 4.557| 3| | 4| 4.352| 5.095| 4.871| 3| | 5| 4.365| 5.140| 4.636| 3|
::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nested |> summarise(across(c(`search reported`, `search's model, honestly`, `no search at all`), mean)) |> round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| search reported| search's model, honestly| no search at all| |---------------:|------------------------:|----------------:| | 4.472| 4.851| 4.471|
::: ::: ## What the results mean The search reported 4.472. The model it chose actually achieves 4.851 — about 8% worse. And doing nothing at all, keeping every real predictor and searching for nothing, achieves 4.471 on the same folds, beating the searched model in **all five**. The reported number is not a lie about arithmetic; the search really did find the lowest cross-validated score among its hundred candidates. It is a lie about the future, because the minimum of a hundred noisy estimates is systematically lower than any of them deserves. The spread the search explored was 0.313 wide, from 4.485 to 4.798. The optimism it created was 0.379. **The search moved the reported number by less than it moved the reported number's error.** Part of that gap is bookkeeping rather than optimism. The nested estimate averages over five large folds rather than ten small ones, and trains on slightly less data; the fold sweep above puts the two together at about 0.04 RMSE. The remaining **0.34 is selection**. So there are three numbers in any tuned analysis, and they are all different: 1. The **score of the winner**, which tells you which candidate to use and nothing else. 2. The **nested estimate**, which tells you how well the whole procedure — search included — will do on new data. 3. The **final model**, which you fit on all the data using the winner's settings, and which has no score of its own at all. Quoting (1) as if it were (2) is the single most common validation error in applied work. ## Where this breaks down Everything on this page assumed that a random division of the rows produces folds that are independent of each other. For survey data that assumption is false, for exactly the reasons [section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd) set out: a station in the held-out fold usually has a near neighbour in the training fold, and repeat visits to one site can be split across both. That does not make the arithmetic on this page wrong. It makes the *question* wrong. Everything here answers "how well does this model predict an unsampled station in the middle of a sampled area", and almost no marine study wants to know that. The [next page](spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) changes the question. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - A single train/test split is a noisy measurement. On this data forty splits of the same 720 stations gave R² anywhere from 0.079 to 0.346; ten-fold cross-validation gave 0.195 to 0.239. - Five or ten folds is a sound default. Two is pessimistic, twenty costs twice as much for no gain, and leave-one-out lands in the same place as ten. - The RMSE `collect_metrics()` reports depends on the number of folds through the averaging alone. Do not compare RMSE across schemes. - The best score from a search is not a performance estimate. Nested cross-validation gives one; here the gap was 8%, and the search lost to not searching at all on every fold. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Rerun the stability comparison with `prop = 0.5` instead of `0.75`. The single-split estimates get worse in two distinct ways — find both. 2. Add `noise_1` through `noise_20` to the *baseline* model in the nested comparison as well, so both arms carry the same junk. How much of the 0.38 gap survives?
